lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: You're listening to Gristwick Parish Radio. Live from the village fête, now in its three hundredth consecutive year.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: Gristwick Parish Radio. Bunting, brass, and a marrow you can see from the next parish.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: This is Gristwick Parish Radio, from the tea tent, where the urn has been on since seventeen twenty six.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: Good morning from Gristwick Parish Radio. The fête is open. The fête is, I'm afraid, still open.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: Gristwick Parish Radio. The fête doesn't close at night. We simply put the fairy lights on, and carry on.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: Some people have asked when the fête will end. It's a fair question. It was a fair question in seventeen fifty. The committee's position is that the fête will close once the tombola has been drawn.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: The tombola has some way to go. There are a great many tickets. Some of them are in Latin.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: The Gristwick Silver Band have been playing the same march since the opening ceremony. They tell me they're nearly at the trio section.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: The trio section is the quiet bit in the middle. They have been looking forward to it for some time. As have we all.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: A good evening to the night operator on the relay ship. We see you pass over the green each night, just above the bunting.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: Do drop in. The fête is open. It is always open. There's a raffle.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: Bev was in the tea tent again this afternoon, asking whether anyone knew a song. It goes, da da dum, da da. The Silver Band said they'd have a go. They've added it to the end of the march.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: So, at the current rate, Bev, we'll get to it in about forty years. Do stay by the radio.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: Every morning, for three hundred years, I have stood on the steps of the tea tent and declared this fête open. And every morning I have rather hoped, just once, to declare it closed.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: I've practised. I know exactly what I'll say. Thank you all. Go home. Mind the bunting.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: One day.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: We had a sudden downpour over the green this afternoon, out of a perfectly clear sky. I'm told it came from a jazz club in a passing cloud, where somebody had applauded.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: We carried on. We always carry on. The cakes were covered in time, and the marrow drank deeply.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: And now, the results from the judging marquee. A great deal of excitement in there this afternoon. Some of it from the judges.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: Results, now, from the fête. Hush in the marquee, please. Mrs Pargeter has the envelopes.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: The giant marrow. Mister Hebblethwaite's marrow was once again too large to bring into the marquee, so the judges went out to it, and were gone some hours.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: They describe it as magnificent, and slightly warm. It has been awarded second place, as ever. First place is being held back, in case it gets bigger. It will.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: The tug of war. Upper Gristwick against Lower Gristwick. The rope was taken up in seventeen eighty, and neither side has moved since.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: The rope is very taut. Both teams are in fine spirits. The judges have declared it a draw for the two hundred and forty sixth year running, and sent sandwiches.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: The Victoria sponge. A strong field this year. The judges tasted forty two sponges. Mrs Pargeter, anything to add?

lines.speaker: Mrs Pargeter, Head Judge
lines.text: We are full.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: First prize to Mrs Abernathy, for a sponge that was light, even and kind. Second, to Mrs Abernathy's sister, who has asked that her objection be noted, for the hundredth year running. It has been.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: The dog show. Dog most like its owner went to a beagle called Admiral, and his owner, also Admiral.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: Waggiest tail went to a spaniel from Lower Hollow called Biscuit, who did not attend, as he is busy watching a hole. The judges felt it was implied.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: The welly throwing. A new record from young Tom Fairley, who threw his boot clean over the church tower. It hasn't come down.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: The judges have agreed to wait for it until the end of the fête. Which may, of course, be a while.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: This afternoon's tombola draw. Ticket number four thousand and twelve, sold in seventeen twenty six, to a lady in a blue bonnet.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: She hasn't come forward. The prize, a bottle of elderflower cordial, is being held for her in the vestry. It has matured considerably.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: Congratulations to all our winners. And to everybody else, there's always next year.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: There is, I'm afraid, always next year.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: Those are the results. Prizes may be collected from the tea tent, where some of them have been waiting since the reign of somebody or other.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: A few notices now, from the fête committee.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: Some announcements, from the steps of the tea tent. Would the band play quietly, please. Thank you. Quieter. Thank you.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: Would the parents of a small boy called Thomas please come to the tea tent. Thomas has been with us since seventeen fifty.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: He's very well. He's now running the tea tent. He asks that you bring your own cup.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: The maypole dancers have asked whether they may stop. The answer, as ever, is after the raffle.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: The maypole is now more ribbon than pole, and has been reclassified by the parish as a large bobbin.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: Raffle tickets are still available from the trestle table by the lych gate. First prize, a hamper. Second prize, last year's hamper.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: Third prize is the hamper from the very first fête, which is not to be opened, and which hums.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: Lost property. A gentleman's top hat, a lady's parasol, a set of keys to a carriage, and a carriage.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: If any of these are yours, please collect them from the vestry. Please also collect the horse.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: The tea tent would like to remind you that the urn has been on since the opening ceremony. The tea is very strong. It is now, I'm told, technically a soup.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: Scones are available, with cream and jam, in whichever order keeps the peace.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: That's all the notices. Do enjoy the fête. You've no choice, but do enjoy it.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: Those are the notices. And please, for the last time this century, keep off the marrow.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: Gristwick Parish Radio. Hello?

lines.speaker: Mr Hebblethwaite
lines.text: Vicar. It's Hebblethwaite.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: Ah, Mister Hebblethwaite. And how is the marrow?

lines.speaker: Mr Hebblethwaite
lines.text: Coming along, Vicar. I've had to move the greenhouse. Well. I've had to move the greenhouse off it.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: Will it be ready for the judging?

lines.speaker: Mr Hebblethwaite
lines.text: Nearly, Vicar. Nearly. Another season or two.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: You said that in seventeen ninety.

lines.speaker: Mr Hebblethwaite
lines.text: And it's been true every time.

lines.speaker: Mr Hebblethwaite
lines.text: Vicar. Can you hear that?

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: Hear what?

lines.speaker: Mr Hebblethwaite
lines.text: That's it growing.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: Lovely, Mister Hebblethwaite. Lovely.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: Good morning. It is my great pleasure, once again, to declare this fête open.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: Again. Thank you.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: The opening ceremony went very well this morning. The ribbon was cut, the band struck up, and a small cheer went up from the regulars, several of whom have been here since the first one.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: I cut the same ribbon every morning. We tie it back together at night. It's very short now.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: A word for anybody arriving at the fête for the first time today. Welcome. Parking is in the top field. Tea is in the tent.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: And the exit is... well. The exit is a matter for the committee.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: Good evening, and welcome to Evensong and Results. The bells are ringing, the band is playing, and the judges have emerged from the marquee, blinking.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: The bells of Saint Wilfreda's are ringing for evensong, as they have every evening of the fête. The bell-ringers have asked me to say that they would quite like to go home.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: I've told them. I know. I know.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: The marquee is emptying after the judging. One of our judges has been judging the jam since seventeen sixty.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: She tells me that, if she's honest, it's all quite good.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: This is the Night Fête, on Gristwick Parish Radio. The fairy lights are on, the urn is on, and the fête, bless it, is on.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: Three in the morning on the green. The band is playing very softly, the dancers are going round the bobbin very slowly, and the urn is ticking away to itself.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: If you're up, come down. We're always up.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: The marrow glows a little at night, I've noticed. Mister Hebblethwaite says that's quite normal, for a marrow of its age.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: I've never met a marrow of its age. I don't believe anyone has.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: For Halloween, the fête committee has carved the prize marrow into a lantern. It took three hundred volunteers and a canal boat. It's lit now. You can see it from the next county.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: Mister Hebblethwaite has asked that nobody tell it what we've done.

clips.title: A Ghost in the Tombola Tent

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: A notice. There is a ghost in the tombola tent. He's a former steward, and he only wants to know whether his ticket won.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: It did, in seventeen ninety. It was a tin of pears. We still have it. We've told him. He isn't convinced. He's staying for the next draw.

lines.speaker: Reverend Clement Ashby
lines.text: Aren't we all.
